title: Azure fundamentals -- resource hierarchy, Subscriptions, Resource Groups
exp: Azure's hierarchy has one genuine structural difference from AWS that trips people up: Resource Groups. Everything else maps cleanly onto concepts you already know.
pts: Management Group: entire divisions of an org, used to apply policy broadly -- large-org concept, skip if not relevant to your context.
Subscription: the billing + fundamental access boundary -- roughly equivalent to an AWS Account.

Resource Group: a project folder inside a subscription. A VM, its storage, its network can all live in one Resource Group -- and deleting the group deletes everything inside it at once. This has NO direct AWS equivalent -- AWS resources aren't grouped this way by default at all.
Hierarchy: Management Group (optional) -> Subscription (billing/access boundary) -> Resource Group (project folder, cascading delete) -> Resources.
Naming and tagging conventions matter more on Azure because Resource Groups become the default cost/access boundary people reason about -- get the grouping right from day one.

Azure resource IDs are hierarchical paths: /subscriptions/{id}/resourceGroups/{rg}/providers/{provider}/{type}/{name} -- the Azure equivalent of an AWS ARN, but always encodes the Resource Group in the path.
code:
# Azure CLI -- fundamentals
az login
az account list --output table
az account set --subscription "Pipeline-Subscription"

# Create the project folder -- everything for this pipeline lives here
az group create --name rg-orders-pipeline --location eastus

# Everything inside rg-orders-pipeline can be deleted in ONE command --
# no AWS equivalent for this cascading behavior
az group delete --name rg-orders-pipeline --yes --no-wait

# Resource ID structure -- the Azure equivalent of an ARN
# /subscriptions/<sub-id>/resourceGroups/rg-orders-pipeline
#   /providers/Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts/satishpipeline
pr: Create a Resource Group, put a storage account inside it, then delete the whole group in one command

r: AWS Resource (EC2 instance, S3 bucket, etc.)

qa.q: What is a Resource Group and why does it have no direct AWS equivalent?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** A Resource Group is a logical container for resources sharing a lifecycle -- typically deployed, managed, and deleted together. AWS has no default equivalent grouping construct at this level; you'd have to build the same 'delete everything for this project at once' behavior yourself via tags and a script, or CloudFormation stack deletion for IaC-managed resources specifically. In Azure, this cascading delete is a first-class, built-in behavior of the platform itself.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** Transient creates a new instance on every request; Scoped creates one instance per HTTP request container; Singleton lives for the app domain lifespan. Capturing a Scoped service inside a Singleton captures the DbContext across requests, causing concurrency bugs.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Instantiating new HttpClient() instances manually causes socket exhaustion in OS TIME_WAIT state under high concurrency. Fix: register typed clients with IHttpClientFactory to manage handler lifetimes and DNS refresh.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** IHttpClientFactory prevents socket leaks and manages DNS rotation, but requires explicit Polly retry and circuit breaker policies to prevent cascade failures during downstream outages.

qa.q: What is the Azure equivalent of an AWS Account, and what's the practical difference in how it's used day-to-day?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** A Subscription is the billing and fundamental access boundary, closely analogous to an AWS Account. The practical difference: within one Subscription, Resource Groups provide a second layer of organization AWS doesn't have natively -- meaning a single Azure Subscription commonly hosts many distinct projects cleanly separated by Resource Group, where the AWS equivalent might require multiple Accounts or careful tagging discipline to achieve the same separation.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** Transient creates a new instance on every request; Scoped creates one instance per HTTP request container; Singleton lives for the app domain lifespan. Capturing a Scoped service inside a Singleton captures the DbContext across requests, causing concurrency bugs.
